project.title: Antifungal Synergy: Mechanistic Insights into the R-1-R Peptide and Bidens pilosa Extract as Potent Therapeutics against Candida spp. through Proteomics
project.projectDescription: Previous work has reported that the peptide derived from LfcinB, R-1-R exhibited anti-Candida activity, which is enhanced when combined with an extract from the Bidens pilosa plant. However, the mechanism of action has not been studied until now. In the current study, an approach to the mechanism of action was carried out through the use of mutant strains of C. albicans, a proteomic approach, followed by a bioinformatic analysis, and a validation of the results obtained, through biological assays in both SC5314 strain and a fluconazole-resistant isolate of Candida albicans, after incubation with the treatments. The results obtained with the mutant strains suggest that the R-1-R peptide and the B. pilosa extract exhibit a mechanism of action related to cell wall stress mediated by MAPKs (Hog1p and Mkc1p) and alteration in mitochondrial respiration due to interruption of ETC.  After, changes in the protein expression profile of FLC-sensitive and -resistant C. albicans after six h of incubation with R-1-R or combination were analyzed, using a label free quantitative proteomic approach. The proteomic data showed that after treatment with R-1-R in the two study strains, most of the differentially expressed proteins in comparison to controls were up-regulated. These proteins were mainly involved in membrane and cell wall biosynthesis, membrane transporters, oxidative stress, the mitochondrial respiratory chain, and response to DNA damage.  Besides, the proteomic analysis of C. albicans parental strain SC5314 treated with R-1-R in combination with an ethanolic extract of B. pilosa was also undertaken. The proteins differentially expressed after this treatment were involved in similar functional processes as the proteins differentially expressed after treatment with R-1-R peptide alone, but at different levels and were mostly down-regulated. The biological assays allowed validation of the proteomic results, evidencing damage to the cell surface, generation of reactive oxygen species and decrease in mitochondrial membrane potential. The results provide information to begin to unlock the understanding of the complex antifungal mode of action of the R-1-R peptide, its combination with the extract, and possibly other derivatives of natural products.
project.sampleProcessingProtocol: Yeast cells (1x107 cell/mL) were pretreated in Roswell Park Memorial Institute (RPMI) 1640 medium (with MOPS, pH 7.2), for 6 h; C. albicans SC5314 was treated with peptide R-1-R (CMI 100 µg/mL) and a combination of R-1-R (25 µg/mL) and an ethanolic extract of B. pilosa leaves (250 µg/mL), where a synergistic effect was previously found. On the other hand, C. albicans 256 was treated only with R-1-R (CMI 100 µg/mL). The concentration values of the evaluated substances used, were previously reported by [13]. The treated cells were washed twice with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). After, the cells were resuspended with lysis buffer [50 mM Tris HCl pH 7.5, 1 mM Ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA), 150 mM NaCl, 1 mM dithiothreitol (DTT), 1 mM phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride (PMSF) and protein inhibitor], later glass beads (0.5-0.78 mm) were added and the sample was taken to a FastPrep equipment (MP Biomedicals, California, United States) (8 cycles of 20 seconds-5.5 speed and cooling on ice, 5 minutes between cycles). Once the extract of cytoplasmic proteins was obtained, this was separated from the glass beads by centrifugation (13000 rpm for 20 min), the supernatant was collected and clarified by centrifugation [62]. The protein concentrations were determined by Bradford Assay, using bovine serum albumin as standard. Then, 1D gel electrophoresis was performed to determine the homogeneity of the samples (10 µg of protein), and the samples were adjusted to 1ug. Four biological replicates were made. Digestion and desalting were carried out on the samples with the PreOmics®' iST Kit according to the protocol of the supplier.
project.dataProcessingProtocol: To the proteomic analysis, peptides were analyzed by RP-LC-ESI-MS/MS using an EASYnLC1000 System coupled to a Q-Exactive-HF mass spectrometer via Nano-Easy spray source (Thermo Scientific, Mississauga, ON, Canada). Peptides were concentrated by reversed phase (RP) chromatography using an Acclaim PepMap 100 precolumn (Thermo Scientific, 20mm x 75 µm ID, C18 3 µm particle diameter and 100 Å pore size) with integrated spray tip, operating at a flow of 250 nL/min. Subsequently, peptides were eluted using a gradient from 5% to 35% buffer B in 220 min, from 35 to 45% in 10 min, from 45 to 95% in 10 min, and 10 min at 95%. As buffer A, 0.1% AF, 2% ACN in water and as buffer B, 0.1% formic acid in ACN were used. The entry of the peptides was carried out by electrospray ionization in positive mode and they were analyzed in a Q Exactive HF mass spectrometer in DDA (data dependent acquisition) mode. From each mass spectrum (MS) scan (between 350 and 1700 Da), the 10 most intense precursors (charge between 2+ and 5+) were selected for HCD (high collision energy dissociation) fragmentation and the corresponding MS/MS spectra were acquired. The data files generated in the shotgun analysis were transferred to the Proteome Discoverer software (Thermo Scientific), where the identification of the PSMs (peptide-spectrum matches) of each MS/MS spectrum was carried out by comparison with the theoretical mass lists corresponding to the mass of the precursor of origin, extracted from Candida Genome Database (CGD) and the contaminant database. The peptides thus identified were assigned to their corresponding proteins. When a peptide can be assigned to several proteins, the software uses the principle of parsimony to generate a “Master” protein that is reported in the results. The percolator algorithm was used to estimate the FDR (false positive rate) and filtered by a q value <0.01 for proteins identified with high confidence. After, data were normalized by the Protein Discoverer software, using a correction factor with the sum of the intensities of all the peptides for each of the samples, and calculating the peptide ratios as the median of the sum of the abundances of each of the replicates of each condition. Finally, the protein ratio was calculated as the geometric median of the peptide group ratios. The statistical analysis used was an Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) to estimate the probability that these measurements are different between conditions, and to find significant comparisons the p-value (p<0.05) obtained in the T-student. This analysis was refined using the Benjamin-Hochberg ad hoc test, achieving an adjusted p-value, also called q-value, (q<0.05) that better controls the FDR. The filters applied to obtain the list of differential proteins (Up and Down regulated proteins) were: (i) Abundance ratio variability: Variability of the ratios calculated as a percentage must present a value below 30% and above 0%. This last case ensured elimination of those proteins that have been quantified from a single measurement. (ii) p-value <0.05, and (iii) q-value <0.05.  Additionally, bioinformatics analysis was made to the differential proteins in the next comparisons, R-1-R peptide vs basal SC5314, Combination vs basal SC5314, R-1-R peptide vs basal. 256. Initially, a functional analysis was made to determine whether both biological functions and known processes were overrepresented in the data set. The functional analysis was carried out using the “gprofiler2” package of RStudio, which allows functional analysis to be performed from a list of protein identifiers using the Ensembl database. The parameters used in the functional analysis were following: Reference organism: “Candida albicans” as a reference organism for the list of protein identifiers, P value: < 0.05, and Multiple testing correction method: FDR. The databases used for the enrichment of biological terms were: Gene Ontology (covering Molecular Function (MF), Cellular Component (CC), and Biological Process (BP), Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG), Reactome (REAC), and WikiPathways (WP). The results were represented by barplots. To predict the protein-protein interaction networks, the STRING database (https://string-db.org/) was used. Finally, to annotate the protein pathway, KEGG (https://www.genome.jp/kegg/) database.
